explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. The text says, "Now the leaders of the people settled in Jerusalem…" (Nehemiah 11:1). The leaders go first, and then everybody else gets in line behind them. I think that's a pretty good way to lead, because nobody can say "you first" when the boss is already unpacking boxes.

Good guess, since a city with a new wall sounds like it needs guards. But the text never mentions royal guards moving in. It says the leaders of the people settled in Jerusalem (Nehemiah 11:1). The gatekeepers do show up later in the roll call, but they're a different group.

Tyre traders do show up in Nehemiah, but not in this passage. Here the text says "the leaders of the people settled in Jerusalem" (Nehemiah 11:1). These are Jerusalem's own folks moving in. No traders, no sales pitch, no "limited time offer."

Yes, friend. The text says the rest of the people "cast lots to bring one out of ten to live in the holy city of Jerusalem…" (Nehemiah 11:1). Casting lots was a way of picking, kind of like drawing names. Nobody had to argue about who was moving, because the lots settled it.

Not this time, friend. The text says the rest of the people "cast lots to bring one out of ten to live in the holy city of Jerusalem…" (Nehemiah 11:1). So the lots did the choosing, and nobody had to pick favorites. That's one way to keep a whole town from fighting over who gets the good spot.

That's it, friend. One out of ten gets picked to live in Jerusalem, "while the remaining nine were to dwell in their own towns" (Nehemiah 11:1). Picture ten people at a table and only one gets the move. I'd be that one nervously checking if my mustache fits through the door.

Three would be a lot more moving boxes, friend. The text says one out of ten, and the remaining nine stay in their own towns (Nehemiah 11:1). So most people kept their homes and only one in every ten packed up for Jerusalem.

Five out of ten would be half the people, and that's not what the text says. It says "one out of ten," and "the remaining nine were to dwell in their own towns" (Nehemiah 11:1). That makes the odds pretty small. I'd feel like I won a raffle I never even entered.
Right, friend. The text calls it "the holy city of Jerusalem" (Nehemiah 11:1). That's the name it carries here, and it's a big one. Moving there meant moving into the city with that name on it.
Royal sounds fancy, I'll give you that. But the text doesn't call Jerusalem the royal city. It says "the holy city of Jerusalem" (Nehemiah 11:1). Holy is the word the writer chose.
Ancient is true in a way, since Jerusalem had been around a long time. But that's not the word the text uses here. It says "the holy city of Jerusalem" (Nehemiah 11:1). Holy is the name on this one.

That's right, friend. The text says, "And the people blessed all the men who volunteered to live in Jerusalem" (Nehemiah 11:2). These men raised their hands when nobody picked them, and the people noticed. I think everybody remembers who stepped up first, like the one person who says "I'll bring the cookies."

Nobody gets a bill here, friend. The text says, "And the people blessed all the men who volunteered to live in Jerusalem" (Nehemiah 11:2). A blessing is a way better welcome gift than a tax form. Nothing in this passage says the volunteers were taxed.

I can see why you'd think so, since moving is hard work. But the text doesn't say the people pitied them. It says, "And the people blessed all the men who volunteered to live in Jerusalem" (Nehemiah 11:2). That sounds a lot more like thanks than pity.
